posts.image_prompt: Endless rows of life-size ancient Chinese clay soldier statues standing in a vast earthen excavation pit, each with a different face, faint traces of red and blue paint, soft overhead light and dust in the air, cinematic wide shot
posts.caption:
🏺 FARMERS DIGGING A WELL FOUND AN ARMY

In March 1974, farmers digging for water near Xi'an, China, struck pieces of a clay figure.

They had found the edge of one of the greatest archaeological discoveries ever: the Terracotta Army, buried to guard the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of a unified China.

Estimates suggest around 8,000 soldiers, along with horses and chariots. Their bodies came from moulds, but their faces vary — no two look quite alike.

They were once brightly painted. Archaeologists report the colours faded quickly once exposed to air.

And the emperor's own burial mound? It has never been opened. The ancient historian Sima Qian wrote that it held rivers of mercury, and soil tests around it have found unusually high mercury levels.

Should archaeologists open the emperor's tomb — or leave it sealed?

posts.caption:
🎻 In 1518, Strasbourg couldn't stop dancing.

It began with one woman in July. Within weeks, chronicles describe hundreds caught up in it. The city even hired musicians to help them 'dance it out'.

Toxic fungus or mass stress? What's your theory? 👇

posts.image_prompt: A French general of the early 1800s in a dark bicorne hat and military greatcoat standing among very tall grenadier guards in bearskin caps on a misty field, illustrating the height contrast, cinematic oil-painting style
posts.caption:
📏 WAS NAPOLEON REALLY SHORT?

Probably not — at least not for his time.

His height was recorded as 5 feet 2 inches. But those were French inches, which were longer than British ones: about 2.71 cm versus 2.54 cm.

Converted, most estimates put him around 5'6" to 5'7" — roughly 1.68 to 1.70 metres. That was average or even a little above average for a Frenchman of his era.

So why the myth? British cartoonists, especially James Gillray, loved drawing him as a tiny, tantrum-throwing 'Little Boney'.

It didn't help that he was often surrounded by his Imperial Guard, who had to meet a height requirement. And his nickname, 'le petit caporal' — the little corporal — was a term of affection, not a measurement.

Which do you think shapes history more: what happened, or the cartoons about it?

posts.title: England's crown jewels vanished in the mud
posts.hook_text: LOST & FOUND? A KING'S MISSING TREASURE

posts.caption:
👑 ON THIS DAY in 1216, King John of England died — days after his baggage train was swept away in the Wash.

Medieval chroniclers said carts, horses and treasure vanished into the tidal sands near King's Lynn. England's crown jewels did disappear around this time, but nobody knows exactly what was lost — and nothing has ever been found.

Do you think the treasure is still down there? 👇

📅 ON THIS DAY in 1781, the British army surrendered at Yorktown — and its commander didn't turn up.

On October 19, 1781, after a siege by American and French forces, more than 7,000 British soldiers marched out to lay down their arms in Virginia.

General Cornwallis stayed away, pleading illness. He sent his deputy, Brigadier General Charles O'Hara, to hand over his sword.

O'Hara first tried to surrender to the French commander, Rochambeau. Rochambeau pointed him to George Washington. Washington refused too: if Cornwallis sent a deputy, a deputy would accept. He signalled to Major General Benjamin Lincoln.

The twist? Seventeen months earlier, Lincoln had been forced to surrender Charleston to the British — and was refused the traditional honours of war.

And that famous story that the British band played "The World Turned Upside Down"? No record from the day says so. It was first written down nearly a century later.

Was Washington's refusal fair protocol — or payback?

posts.title: Escape from Alcatraz: How Three Men Vanished from 'The Rock' in 1962
posts.hook_text: THREE MEN. ONE RAFT. NEVER FOUND.

scenes.narration: On the morning of June 12, 1962, guards at Alcatraz made their bed check. Three prisoners didn't move. Their heads were fake.
scenes.label: 12 JUN 1962

scenes.narration: Frank Morris and brothers John and Clarence Anglin had broken out of America's most famous prison. They have never been seen again, dead or alive.
Stay with us to see how they did it with spoons and raincoats, the clues the bay gave up, and why the case is still open today.
Alcatraz sat on a rocky island in San Francisco Bay. The cold water and fast tides around it were meant to make escape close to impossible.
scenes.label: SAN FRANCISCO

scenes.narration: Morris and the Anglins were not violent killers. They were bank robbers, sent to Alcatraz because they kept escaping from other prisons.
A fourth inmate, Allen West, was part of the plan. He would later claim the whole escape had been his idea, though officials doubted him.
Their route out was simple to describe and hard to reach: through the walls, up to the roof, down to the shoreline, then across the open water of the bay.
For about six months, they widened the small air vents at the back of their cells, using saw blades, metal spoons from the dining hall, and a homemade drill.
scenes.label: 6 MONTHS

scenes.narration: That drill was built from the motor of a vacuum cleaner. Behind the vents ran a utility corridor, and from there they could climb up inside the cell block.
Above the cell block they set up a hidden workshop. There they built a raft and life vests from more than fifty stolen raincoats.
The seams were sealed with heat from the prison's steam pipes. They made paddles from plywood, and a musical instrument was converted to pump air into the raft.
To fool the night guards, they sculpted heads from soap, toothpaste, concrete dust and toilet paper, painted them, and added real hair from the prison barbershop.
On the night of June 11, the three men crawled out through their vents. Allen West could not: hardened cement had narrowed his opening, and he was left behind.
scenes.label: 11 JUN 1962

scenes.narration: The other three climbed up to the roof through a ventilator, crossed it in the dark, and slid down a bakery smokestack to the ground.
At the shoreline, they inflated their raft and pushed off into the dark. Angel Island lay about two miles to the north.
scenes.label: 2 MILES

scenes.narration: The tides there are powerful. Strong currents could have carried a small raft past the Golden Gate and out into the Pacific in under an hour.
The search began at once. Investigators recovered pieces of paddles and rubber debris from the water, and a packet of sealed personal letters.
A life vest washed up on Cronkhite Beach, beyond the Golden Gate. A paddle like one of theirs was found near Angel Island.
scenes.label: CLUES

scenes.narration: Allen West, the man left behind, talked. He gave investigators details of the plan, from the vents to the raft.
The FBI concluded the men most likely drowned. No cars or clothes were reported stolen, no family help was found, and no credible sign they were alive ever emerged.
Less than a year later, on March 21, 1963, Alcatraz closed for good, because it was too expensive to run and salt water was eating away the buildings.

The FBI closed its file at the end of 1979, the same year Clint Eastwood played Frank Morris in the film Escape from Alcatraz. But the U.S. Marshals never closed theirs. The warrants for the three men remain active.
So: did they drown in the bay that night, or reach shore and live quietly for decades? What's your verdict? Follow for more untold history.

posts.caption:
🔓 Three men. One raft made of raincoats. Never found.

On June 11, 1962, Frank Morris and John and Clarence Anglin crawled out of their cells on Alcatraz — leaving fake heads in their beds made of soap, toothpaste and real human hair.

This documentary follows the six months of planning, the night of the escape, the clues that washed up afterwards, and why U.S. Marshals still haven't closed the case.

Did they drown that night, or make it to shore?
